FamilySearch collection 1417683 is name-searchable. This item serves as the required FAN search for this parentage question (BCG Standard 14).

A will or estate administration for Thomas Flynn filed with the Schuylkill County Register of Wills would be direct parentage evidence if it names Patrick as a son and heir. Schuylkill County probate records are available from the county's formation in 1811. The date range 1860–1900 is set to Thomas's plausible death window: born ~1818, he could have died from his early 40s through his early 80s. Source S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already cited in the project tree. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); a dedicated browse volume (image group 007936749, covering 1851–1930) is also available. Browse dockets for Thomas Flynn and variant Flinn.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother — a required item for every parentage plan (Appendix B). The date range 1840–1855 is set to Thomas's likely marriage window: born ~1818, Patrick born ~1845, so marriage probably ~1838–1844. If Thomas and his wife married in Ireland before immigrating, no Pennsylvania church marriage record will exist, but the Schuylkill County church records browse volume (image group 007936751, covering 1842–1895, browse-only (personCount 0)) is worth checking. Schuylkill County Roman Catholic parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (loc_001); sacramental registers are held at the parish. This record supplies the mother's maiden name, the key unknown for the parentage question, and confirms Thomas and the mother as a married couple — though it does not by itself place Patrick in their family. Note: if the mother had a prior marriage, the surname this record gives her may be a prior married name rather than her birth name; pair with a search for any earlier Flynn-area marriage if the name found differs from what the death cert or census records show.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record in Schuylkill County, if he married there, may name both of his parents on the license or register. The Schuylkill County civil and church marriage records browse volume (image group 007936753, covering 1870–1910, browse-only (personCount 0)) covers his most likely marrying years. A marriage record also corroborates identity by linking Patrick to a spouse and place across time, and may supply a residence or church affiliation that points toward additional records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position consistent with child
items.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1850 census
items.informant_bias_notes: 1850 census does not state relationships; this assertion is inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly reported by any informant. The relationship is indirect evidence constructed by the researcher, not information provided by a census informant.

items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

entry.rationale: The 1880 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1417683) is name-searchable. Unlike the 1850 (S1) and 1860 (S2) censuses already in the tree — both of which list household members without stating relationships — the 1880 schedule explicitly records each person's relationship to the head of household. Searching for Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) in Schuylkill County should produce his household; if his wife was still living, she will be named, identifying Patrick's mother. The existing census sources (S1, S2) show co-residence but the 1860 census does not name Thomas's wife. Try variant spellings Flynn and Flinn.

The 1870 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. This decade falls between the 1860 census already in the tree (S2) and 1880, providing an intermediate household snapshot. The 1870 schedule names all household members with age and birthplace; Thomas Flynn's wife (Patrick's mother) would appear if living. Try variant spellings Flynn and Flinn.

The 1900 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) would be approximately 55 and should appear; Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) would be approximately 82 and may still be living. The 1900 schedule records years of immigration, years of marriage, number of children born and surviving — all potentially constraining Thomas's marriage and family. Searching both Patrick's and Thomas's entries may name the mother.

The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0) — this requires an image browse of the county docket volumes, not a name search. Per loc_001, Schuylkill County probate records are held by the Register of Wills from 1811. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) already appears in the project's source descriptions but is not linked to any assertion; this item executes that browse. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) is the candidate father; his will or administration, if found, would directly name his heirs — including Patrick as a son — and typically names his wife, identifying Patrick's mother. Date range set to Thomas's plausible lifespan as the record's creator (not Patrick's research window).

For a parentage question, a dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other is required. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) married before Patrick's birth (~1845); a Catholic parish marriage register entry would supply the mother's maiden name — information no census records. Per loc_001, RC parishes in Schuylkill County fall under the Diocese of Philadelphia (not Scranton, which was erected in 1868 for the northern counties only). The couple's marriage confirms them as a unit and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates Thomas as a father otherwise named only by indirect census co-residence and a derivative death certificate, but the marriage record alone does not establish that Patrick is their child — a record placing Patrick with them is still needed. Note: the family was in Pennsylvania by 1850 and Thomas was born ~1818 in Ireland; the marriage may predate immigration, but searching Schuylkill County registers is the first step. Try Flynn and Flinn.

Per loc_001, Pennsylvania statewide civil death registration did not begin until 1906; Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) most likely died before 1906, making a church burial record the primary death evidence. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. A burial entry may record the spouse's name or note survivors, helping identify Patrick's mother. Date range bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan as the record's creator. Try Flynn and Flinn.

For a parentage question, at least one FAN item is required. Searching the 1850 and 1860 censuses for other Flynn households in the same Schuylkill County neighborhoods as Thomas Flynn (near dwelling 84 in 1850 per S1, near dwelling 112 in 1860 per S2) may identify siblings of Thomas or Patrick who share the same parents, providing collateral corroboration of parentage. Irish immigrants frequently settled near relatives or neighbors from the same Irish townland. A sibling's household naming the same father or mother would be independent evidence of the family unit. Try Flynn and Flinn.

The United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865 (collection 1910717) is name-searchable. Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) was approximately 16-20 years old during the Civil War; Schuylkill County, an anthracite coal region, raised numerous Pennsylvania infantry regiments. A compiled service record confirms identity. If Patrick applied for a pension, the pension file would name next of kin and potentially his parents, providing additional parentage evidence.

Pennsylvania deed books require a wife's signature or explicit dower release when a married man conveys real property; a deed naming Thomas Flynn and his wife would directly identify Patrick's mother by her given name. Per loc_001, Schuylkill County is the jurisdictional unit for land records from 1811. This item falls back from the probate search: if Thomas left no will or administration, land deed records may be the next best source for naming his wife. Search FamilySearch first; if unavailable, county deed books are held at the Schuylkill County courthouse.

**Plan pl_001 created for q_001 — "Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. c. 1843, Baiersbronn)?"**

---

**What the tree currently shows:**
- Katharina Seeger (I1): born about 1843, Baiersbronn, Württemberg — no parents, no sources attached.

**Key locality finding:**
Civil registration didn't begin in Württemberg until 1876, so Katharina's 1843 birth is covered only by church records. The Protestant parish registers for Baiersbronn are digitized on **Archion** (a paid German church-archive site) at:
> https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn

---

**4-Step Research Plan (all on Archion):**

| # | Record Type | Date Range | What to Look For |
|---|-------------|------------|-----------------|
| pli_001 | **Familienregister** | 1800–1870 | Browse "S" entries for Seeger/Seger — one entry should list the parents and all their children, including Katharina ~1843 |
| pli_002 | **Taufen (Baptisms)** | 1841–1845 | Find Katharina's baptism entry, which directly names father and mother |
| pli_003 | **Heiraten (Marriages)** | 1820–1843 | Find the parents' marriage entry to confirm the couple and get the mother's maiden name |
| pli_004 | **Heiraten (FAN/siblings)** | 1855–1890 | Browse for other Seeger/Seger brides or grooms — potential siblings whose entries also name the same parents |

---

**What you need to do:**

1. **Log into Archion** at the link above with your personal subscription.
2. **Start with the Familienregister** — page through "S" entries; this is the highest-efficiency starting point since one entry typically covers the whole family.
3. **Check the 1841–1845 baptism register** for Katharina's entry — this is primary evidence.
4. **Browse marriages 1820–1843** for a Seeger/Seger bridegroom to confirm the parents as a couple and capture the mother's maiden name.
5. **Browse marriages 1855–1890** for potential siblings as a corroborating source.

When you find relevant pages, **photograph or screenshot** the entries and bring them back — they can then be recorded as evidence toward answering the parentage question.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Per loc_001, the county Register of Wills held these from 1811 onward. Browse image by image; search under Flynn and variants Flinn, Flin.

The Schuylkill County anthracite coal region drew large numbers of Irish Catholic immigrants; Thomas and Patrick Flynn's Irish birth is established by the 1850 and 1860 censuses. FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). Sacramental registers — baptisms, confirmations, marriages, burials — for the Flynn family may name parents, give ages, or supply the mother's maiden name. Per loc_001, RC parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (Archdiocese from 1875). Include spelling variants Flynn, Flinn.

Volume 007936751 (Schuylkill County church records, 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0). Per loc_001, some anthracite-region church films are not name-indexed and must be browsed image by image. Search this volume if the name-searchable collection (item 2) returns no Flynn entries.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother is required for this parentage plan. The couple's marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name, which census and death records typically omit, and confirms the couple as a unit. Thomas born ~1818 likely married in the late 1830s or early 1840s; any Pennsylvania church marriage could appear in the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection (name-searchable, personCount 982,415) or the marriage volume 007936753 (browse-only, personCount 0). Note: this record establishes the couple — it does not, by itself, prove Patrick is their child; a record placing Patrick in their household remains necessary for that link.

The 1880 census is the first U.S. census to record each person's relationship to the head of household, making it the highest-value census for direct parentage evidence. The timeline (t_001) shows a HIGH severity gap from 1860-1908 with 1880 listed as an expected event. If Patrick and Thomas appear in the same 1880 household, the relationship column gives direct evidence of the father-son link. Collection 'United States Census, 1880' (1417683) is name-searchable (personCount 50,169,452). Thomas Flynn would be ~62, Patrick ~35.

A dedicated search for Patrick Flynn's marriage is required for this parentage plan. A marriage record routinely states age and birthplace, corroborating Patrick's identity across the HIGH gap (t_001, 1860-1908). The Schuylkill County marriage records volume 007936753 (1870-1910) is browse-only (personCount 0). The SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection may also contain marriage registers. Search from 1865 (Patrick ~20) through 1900; the record may also name parents or a home parish.

The timeline (t_001) flags 1870 as an expected event in the HIGH severity gap (1860-1908). Patrick (~25) and Thomas (~52) should appear in Schuylkill County. While 1870 does not state relationships, co-residence corroborates the parent-child link established by the 1850 and 1860 censuses. Collection 'United States Census, 1870' (1438024) is name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371).

The timeline (t_001) flags 1900 as an expected event in the HIGH severity gap; Patrick died in 1908, so the 1900 census should show him. The 1900 census states number of years in the US and immigration year, corroborating Patrick's Irish birth (established by the 1850 and 1860 censuses). Collection 'United States Census, 1900' (1325221) is name-searchable (personCount 76,211,837).

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 and would have been 16-20 during the Civil War. A service or pension record could give his birthplace, physical description, and age, and pension applications sometimes name parents or siblings. This also fills the HIGH gap window (t_001) where Patrick's whereabouts between 1860 and 1908 are otherwise untracked. Collection 'United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865' (1910717) is name-searchable (personCount 6,282,360).

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

---

### Key context from the tree

- Michael has an unsourced 1870 Pennsylvania residence, an unsourced 1882 Schuylkill County residence, and an unsourced "Miner" occupation in 1882.
- Sibling **Patrick Sheahan** already had a Schuylkill County deed in 1875 (sourced, S1) — an established family pull factor predating Michael's move.

---

### Research Plan pl_001 — 8 items in sequence

| # | Type | Place | Repository | Date range | Purpose |
|---|------|--------|------------|------------|---------|
| pli_001 | Census | Pennsylvania | FamilySearch | 1880 | Closest anchor before the move; where was Michael & what was his occupation? |
| pli_002 | Census | Pennsylvania | FamilySearch | 1870 | Source the unsourced F1 residence; was mining already his trade? |

| pli_004 | Census | Pennsylvania | FamilySearch | 1900 | "Years at current address" column directly dates the settlement |

| pli_008 | Land/Deeds | Schuylkill Co. | FamilySearch | 1880–1900 | Property transaction as independent arrival timeline *(fallback for pli_001)* |

### Next step

Run the **FamilySearch name searches** first: pli_001, pli_002, pli_003, pli_004, pli_005, and pli_008 (all searchable on FamilySearch). Items pli_006 (Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg) and pli_007 (browse-only images) require separate handling.

response.objective: Determine why Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882

openQuestions.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

questionStatuses.nextStep: research-plan

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The tree records Michael's Schuylkill County residence in 1882 (F2) and his occupation as Miner (F3), but neither fact is sourced. The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683) is name-searchable and was taken two years before the alleged move. It will show where Michael actually lived in 1880 — if not yet in Schuylkill County, it establishes the move did occur between 1880 and 1882; if already there, it pushes the move earlier than family tradition holds. His stated occupation in 1880 tests whether mining was his work before or only after settling in Schuylkill County. Search on 'Sheahan' and the variant 'Sheehan' in Pennsylvania. The 1880 schedule records each person's relationship to the household head, which may reveal co-residence with Patrick (I2).

The tree records a 1870 Pennsylvania residence for Michael (F1), but that fact is unsourced and gives only the state — not the county. The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Finding Michael in 1870 will source this fact, establish his precise county, and record his occupation 12 years before the alleged Schuylkill County move. If he was already listed as a miner in a different Pennsylvania county in 1870, it suggests he was a traveling mine worker who later relocated; if he was in a non-mining occupation, it supports the interpretation that the move specifically corresponded with taking up anthracite mining. Search 'Sheahan' and 'Sheehan' across Pennsylvania. The 1870 schedule also records each household member's birthplace — useful for confirming Irish origin.

FAN item targeting Patrick Sheahan (I2, sibling of Michael). Patrick is already documented in Schuylkill County by 1875 via a deed purchase (Deed Book 42 p. 118, S1). An established sibling working in a coal-mining community is a classic pull factor for a subsequent family migration. The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683) is name-searchable; finding Patrick in Schuylkill County in 1880 and recording his stated occupation will confirm whether the sibling was embedded in the mine-worker community that may have drawn Michael there around 1882 — direct evidence bearing on the reason for Michael's move, not merely on Patrick's own genealogy. Search 'Sheahan' and 'Sheehan' in Schuylkill County.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. It is the first federal census that asks all foreign-born persons how many years they have resided in the United States, and it also records the number of years at the current address — both fields bearing directly on when Michael arrived in Schuylkill County and whether he was foreign-born. His occupation in 1900 will confirm sustained mine work in the years following the 1882 move. Combined with the 1880 census result (item 1), these two records bracket the migration window and could narrow 'around 1882' to a specific span. Search 'Sheahan' and 'Sheehan' in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

The Sheahan surname is Irish; Irish immigrants in the Schuylkill County anthracite region were predominantly Roman Catholic. Catholic sacramental registers were kept at the parish level under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875 onward, as the loc_001 entry notes; the Diocese of Scranton erected in 1868 did not include Schuylkill County). The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) is name-searchable. A baptism, marriage, or burial entry for Michael Sheahan could record his birthplace, prior parish, or year of arrival in the county — evidence directly bearing on his origin and the timing of the move. Note that PA civil registration did not begin until 1906 (loc_001 quirk), so church records are the primary vital-events source for this period. Search 'Sheahan' and 'Sheehan'.

The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mine Inspection published annual reports beginning in 1870, documenting conditions, fatalities, and — in detailed years — employment rolls at individual collieries in Schuylkill County. These are the most direct source for confirming that Michael Sheahan worked as an anthracite coal miner: a name in the colliery rolls would provide primary occupational evidence for the family tradition, going beyond the census occupation field which is a self-reported derivative. The reports are held by the Pennsylvania State Archives (Commonwealth Keystone Building, Harrisburg) and selected years have been digitized by archive.org and the Hagley Museum and Library. Search by colliery name and year once the specific mine district is known from the census results (items 1-4).

If Michael was Irish-born (as the Sheahan surname strongly suggests), he would have filed a Declaration of Intent and a Petition for Naturalization in Schuylkill County. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records (image group 007936750, 1849-1915) are browse-only (personCount 0) — browsing image by image is required, consistent with the loc_001 quirk that some naturalization films for the anthracite region are 0% record-searchable. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, 1708-1985) contains baptism and christening registers. Since Pennsylvania had no civil birth registration until 1906 (loc_001), Catholic parish baptism entries are the primary original source for each child's birth. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
